title: Is it me or is Wes Anderson just not as great as a I thought he was?

commenti.body:
I think he came out of the gate with 9/10 command over images/editing/composition and has only improved over time. 

I also think his films' narratives have not improved. I am partial to Field Maloney's argument that his writing partnership with Owen Wilson was the secret to his early film's success:

https://slate.com/culture/2005/07/owen-wilson-s-writing-career.html

Asteroid City isn't style over substance, there are both. If anything, Wes Anderson stagnates in his styles mostly. He doesn't try to radically change, because he doesn't try to radically attract attention to his style. The dialogues matter most in Asteroid City, and more than the lines, the backstory of the characters.

And I think that's the main thing with Wes Anderson that we have to understand to appreciate AC. There's a feeling that a character *IS* his backstory, which is a choice that Anderson made consciously. All of the Asteroid City stories relate to this feeling of nostalgia that we experience when we realize that we're just the sum of our context.

The visual impression of the pinks, the neat shapes and composition, the objectification of the set and the props, all of that comes to give this overwhelming sensation that life is "made up". Wes Anderson is actually sacrificing his visual style, in a way.

Same thing for the passages in black and white about the author. This isn't really about an author as much as it is about how *WE* narrate a life to ourselves to keep the lie going. It's black and white because it's overthinking, and we have this drowsiness of feeling empowered by our own planning, and of course Wes Anderson doesn't exclude himself of this critic since he places the author-character at the center of this arc. He is admitting to being the most overthinking person in the room.

Now, a lot of viewers have taken this feeling that Wes Anderson was overthinking, which is admitted by him, and used it as an argument against his film, making this odd conclusion that Wes Anderson was only style. I don't feel that's the case because the whole invention in his plot, the part within Asteroid City, comes off as a dissection of his true inner emotional state. It's rare to have movies that are confessions of their author to this point, and imo it's a nice touch of sincerity that Hollywood nowadays avoids completely, which is too bad.

I’ve never really been a fan of WA but he seems to be leaning so much harder in to the cinematography of the film that it’s affects the core script that he has.  I think he’s an amazing  cinematography but hasn’t rounded out the other areas of directing.  People were just shocked about the visuals early on in his career to overlook his flaws.
[removed]

I'm confused by how you are complaining that Wes Anderson is no longer making the type of movies of his you used to like, but that he's also the type of artist who doesn't change things up. To me that makes it sound like something about his work has changed, and you don't like the direction he's gone in. 

To me, a lot of his work has been about the inability to get at our emotions, or how hard it is to communicate. I think of French Dispatch and Asteroid City as really aggressively pushing this investigation, where the emotional core of the movie is so deeply buried, that many people seem to miss it. His characters can't say what they want to, or don't know how to take what inside them an make it understood by others, and so they evade, mannerisms, affectations are piled on, and this is mirrored in the film through the addition of elaborate frame texts, of lush texture, of distractions, to bury the pain at the core of these movies.

Oh yeah I definitely think there was something to his and Owen's partnership is highly overlooked when looking at the trajectory of WA's career. Honestly I don't know if it's because Owen's made the decision to not really try to bask in the credit of writing some really good stuff, instead being more content to be known as an actor and kind of a bit as a meme (with the much appropriated Owen Wilson voice that you hear so many do).

To me the gimmick is up. I feel like he kinda peaked with Grand Budapest hotel. Conventional effects, highly attentive art direction, quirky characters and dialogue only go so far. It’s kind of cute and engrossing from an aesthetic standpoint but the stories grow a little dull and I find myself becoming emotionally detached and disinterested in some of his movies. 

I’d be really curious to see what he does outside of his usual quirky comedy genre. Like a dramatic period piece written by someone else or a horror movie. 

I think the mark of a good director is when they do a good job with different genres. Kubrick made one of the best sci fi movies of all time, one of the best war movies of all time, one of the best…..whatever the hell Eyes Wide Shut was of all time.

Personally, I think there was so much heart in most of his films leading up to Grand Budapest, which was his magnum opus. 

It’s probably coincidental, but at that point *Wes Anderson style* went very mainstream and his subsequent films feel style over substance because of that.

The French Dispatch is actually a very personal movie for him, it’s borderline autobiographical (at least in the sense that it’s a movie about his love for the New Yorker). 

But that in and of itself sorta leads me back to your side. The last few do feel shallower than say Tenenbaums or Life Aquatic

>The epitome of style over substance.

This is a valid critique in a world in which Wes Anderson is not trying to bring his style to mainstream audiences.

His films have always been heavily reliant on style over substance and some people greatly appreciate his style.

Rushmore would have been a basic story if it had not been for the style complementing the substance. The Royal Tennenbaums would be basically unwatchable if it didn't lean into style over substance.

The Life Aquatic was the epitome of style over substance and I still love turning it on when I want to listen to French renditions of David Bowie alongside a nonsensical plot.

All that said, I agree with you that Wes Anderson is style over substance, but I don't think that is as valid a critique in art as it is in logic and rhetoric.

Can anyone answer this for me?

Why does Wes Anderson always have an animal die in his movies.  Every single movie an animal dies.  Idk when I noticed it but his last few movies or so going in ai thought, I bet an animal dies.  

It's almost never shown too. Just talked about.  The only ones shown would be Buckley in The Royal Tenambaums, and the rat in Fantastic Mr. Fox.

What do you guys think this is about?  What does it represent?  Is it the same message across all movies?  Thank you

Perhaps I'll have to try Asteroid City with what you've wrote and have that in mind, but to me when I think of a movie as a confession of it's author, I think of something like Apocalypse Now by Coppola or The Irishman by Scorsese, where the director is reckoning with something inside of him. 

Maybe it's because I've never gotten the sense that his movies as of late are really reckoning with much of anything. They just seem like exercises in style, like perhaps one could say of a bit of Elvis Costello's career after the first break up with the Attractions, or with David Bowie's entire career. But with those guys, even if the style was coming first at certain points in their career, the changing styles seemed to come from a musical restlessness, which Wes Anderson seems not to have filmmaking wise, as I've said with his stagnant visual style.

And while I'm at it, it's not only the visuals. It's the dialogue. The droll, dry, flat affect. I admit, at first getting into his work it made it feel fresh and different. But just like his visual style, he not only ran with it, but drove it so far into the ground that it's a joke at this point. Not everybody has to have be in the deadpan Bill Murray style. I get why it worked with Bill, because that's a facet of what really works for him. It works for someone quirky like Owen Wilson. But once again, it's just so very overdone.

But here I am again, I'm wishing Anderson would be different from what he is? Maybe I should just leave his stuff alone and not bother? Or is it disappointment that a previous favorite isn't cutting it for me? Maybe it's me more than him?

Anyways, as I said maybe I will try to experience Asteroid City through the lens you see it through. But I admit, knowing what I know about Anderson and his style, it's hard for me to put the words Wes Anderson and "sincerity" together, as I feel that everything about his last two or three films are just so very drenched in that "affect" I've spoken of.
The >!dog<! in *Moonrise Kingdom* also dies, as well as >!one of Steve’s cat (“Marmalade”)<! in *The Life Aquatic*. Wes loves heavy pangs of sadness, and what better way to achieve them?

Nope you're totally wrong. I am not complaining for a second that Wes Anderson isn't making the type of movies I used to like. In fact, I wonder that if I were truly able to take my nostalgia glasses off, whether I would like those movies anymore. But of course those films are now tied in with memories old friends of mine (some who've now passed on), memories of different times, and what-have-you, and that's impossible to separate from the movies themselves.

And no, I don't feel like anything has changed in his movies for the most part. And I think that's why his movies have committed one of the worst sins in film, being BORING. I'd rather have a director or actor or musician shoot for the moon and miss rather than stagnate and make the same piece over and over.
The >!dog!< in *Moonrise Kingdom* also dies, as well as >!one of Steve’s cat (“Marmalade”)!< in *The Life Aquatic*. Wes loves heavy pangs of sadness, and what better way to achieve them?

I agree that perhaps Budapest was his magnum opus. What a picture. Ralph Fiennes is just unbelievably great in it. 

And I even get that Dispatch was his love letter to the New Yorker and whatnot, and I even fully understood that each section was a different section of that magazine. But, to what end? I just don't think it packed an emotional punch at the end of the day.

Boom. You nailed it. You couldn't put Kubrick in a box. Tell me how 2001, Eyes Wide Shut,  Full Metal Jacket and The Shining all fit together: you got me there?

And I don't even LOVE Spielberg (though he has quite a few GREAT pictures), but yeah, if I didn't know better I'd have no clue that the the guy who directed Schindler's List could or would direct Jaws or first three Indiana Jones movies (yes I know he did the fourth as well).

These directors showed true RANGE. Even in just 2014 and 2015 alone, Alejandro Iñárritu released two masterpieces, Birdman and The Revenant, that couldn't seem any more different in aesthetics and general overall feel. I don't think Wes Anderson could do something like if his life depended on it.

I like most of his films, but Asteroid City lost me completely. I felt sadness not in the film’s arc, but in that a director with a style of his own and an impressive portfolio made a rote film that was somehow uninspired but also came off (to me) as entirely arrogant and condescending. 

What I love about WA is he marries a boxed in quality of fantastic traditional theater, but using the grandiosity of Hollywood budgets to emphasize what makes the stage interesting, dynamic, but sometimes wooden and flawed (an off day performance, for instance. Good theater cannot transcend its harshest barrier; human error) He very much carved out his own explicit vision in filmmaking, much like Kubrick; but also unlike Kubrick, it has not evolved over time. 

I say all this not being his biggest fan from the starting gun. I loved the Royal T, and Fantastic Mr Fox is absolutely wonderful to view on a rainy day. However, I do appreciate the niche he carved as a director, but feel it ultimately falls flat without compelling characters, a good plot, and a strong emotional foundation. To me, AC lacked all of that. It came off to me as an atrophied flex. I really wanted to be invested in the fantastical set pieces and atmosphere, but I was ultimately bitten by the sheer robotics of the performances. It kind of reminded me of wandering through the Cars world at Disneyland where everyone was trying to convince me that Cars was the greatest film of all time. That really sounds weird now, even typing it out… but that’s a genuine allocation of my feelings towards that movie. It’s one of the few films that I quiet after less than half the run time.
[removed]

I liked Rushmore. I liked The French Dispatch as a paean to writing and passionate intellectualism and I liked The Grand Budapest Hotel as a big piece of style and wit, but I’m in no hurry to rewatch either. I remember disliking The Life Aquatic which I’ve largely forgotten. The Darjeeling Limited was the last of his I watched. It didn’t engage me. I didn’t care at all about the brothers or their grief. (It doesn’t help that Owen Wilson is a stumbling block for me in any movie, I just don’t like him as an actor.)

I was feeling this way too. The last two films have been somewhat hollow. However, upon rewatching GBH brought me back. It’s a masterpiece, incredibly moving. The essay on the criterion release really helped me understand the work that inspired the film and honestly it left me devastated.

Here’s my take on Anderson: he just doesn’t have much to say. He’s a creative, and he’s very talented. But since he doesn’t have much to really share about the human experience, there’s not a whole lot that can come out. This is where Bottle Rocket and Rushmore seem the most honest and have the most to share. But quite simply none of his films are profound — the closest to that being his first two, as mentioned. 

Compare the depth of a Wes Anderson to Tarkovsky, to Spike Lee at his heights, to David Lynch, to Parajanov, to Mizoguchi, to so many others who are deep thinkers, and who have something profound to share. Just not a whole lot there.

>I think the mark of a good director is when they do a good job with different genres.

Why?

I can appreciate how that's impressive... but we don't complain that Picasso or Rembrandt didn't make enough marble statues.  We aren't asking Bob Dylan to make a rap album.  Voltaire isn't condemned because he "only knew satire."

I can appreciate an artist that wants to be less specialized... but I can appreciate an artist that is completely specialized, too.

Honestly, I don't want to probably even see Woody Allen make a horror film...
Robert David Yeoman

He Wes Anderson'ed too close to the sun. He's the SNL bit you loved for a couple seasons but it ran it's course. He desperately needs a new approach to everything that isn't visual, which to his credit is more important in his films than in most directors who are known for their writing.

I'm really going to have to figure out how to defend Asteroid City because I think it is obviously a great film. Certainly the greatest film I saw this year. But clearly it doesn't resonate with a lot of people. 

People sometimes act like Anderson's films aren't emotional because his characters don't scream their emotions out loud. But this is nonsense. Sure Asteroid City (like many of Anderson's films) about a bunch of repressed people who are scared of facing their real feeling and confronting their real problems. But that isn't a flaw in Asteroid City. That's one of its strengths. 

For me Asteroid City is Anderson's densest and most interesting movie. It's the one I have the hardest time summing up. But here are some topics it tackles:

Asteroid City is a political film about the horrors of WW2 and both its political consequences and its personal consequences in the Cold War.

It's also movie about art and artist and the interrelation between the two. 

It's also a film about childhood, parents and children, and of course grief. 

It's hard for me to think a movie tackling so many important subjects could be a triumph of style over substance.

Like were you just not paying attention or what.

Also just a side note: Bottle Rocket is a cute amateur film and Asteroid City is the work of a master. There is no comparison over quality. But I agree that if you think Bottle Rocket is one of the best Wes Anderson movies, then you probably aren't going to like Wes Anderson.

Just one more addendum. You cannot tell me Wes Anderson's style has stagnated. There has been an obvious growth in Anderson's style towards a more and more abstract/minimalist style. 

If you look at The Royal Tenenbaum's and compare it to Asteroid City or the French Dispatch, this change is quite clear. Certainly there is some artifice in The Royal Tenenbaums but much less than in Asteroid City. The characters are also more expressive there than the are now. The sets are more real than they are now, etc. 

You may not like the direction Anderson has gone. But he definitely has gone in a specific direction.

I think comparing The French Dispatch to Asteroid City is a little like comparing Birdman to Batman. I didn’t think The French Dispatch was all that great, it felt for me a little bit tired and that the concept and style was exhausted with little reinvention and I felt from the trailers for Asteroid City that we were in for more of the same. 

And granted, Asteroid City is far from a perfect film, and in how it’s flawed relative to how self aware it is can be up for debate. BUT…I did think this film at least understood its narrative and stylistic limitations and Anderson tries to directly address them. Successfully for me, I might say. 

With all of that out of the way, yes, it becomes implicitly clear to me that Wes Anderson is either limited to or only interested in telling stories in his own way and style, and I don’t necessarily think Asteroid City marks a creative turning point just yet, but we’ll see.

I like Wes Anderson as a director for maintaining a distinctive personal style, especially in an era where mainstream cinema tends to become more homogenized.  Among his works, I consider "The Grand Budapest Hotel" to be one of his most accomplished films.  


However, I've noticed a shift in his subsequent live-action films. While Anderson continues to deliver visually stunning and unique narratives, there seems to be a missing element – a central protagonist that the audience can truly engage with. Films like "The French Dispatch" and "Astoroyd City" exemplify this absence of a clear focal character.  
In some instances, films like "Short Cuts" or "Magnolia" successfully manage multiple storylines leading to a dramatic conclusion. However, this doesn't seem to be the primary focus of Anderson's recent works. It's as if the charm of a central character, which was evident in his earlier films, is somewhat diluted in these later output. It leaves me wondering if the lack of a strong central figure affects the overall impact of his storytelling in these more recent projects.

A while ago I listened to an interview with Garth Jennings (director of Son of Rambo etc) and he told a story about how Wes Anderson & Sofia Coppola had invited him and his girlfriend / wife / kids (I can’t remeber exactly) to come and stay with them. They basically hire out some grand building or luxury villa somehwere and 'holiday' there with various people. Inviting friends & family members, along with whoever they think may make interesting guests from the industry. It sounded incredibly opulent and lavish, yet for them a banally normal event. Jennings not being the Hollywood type found it kinda surreal & felt somewhat out of place. It left me with the impression that obviously that’s the kind of incredibly existence that they're used to and that maybe the kind of opulent, grandiose, disconected nature of Anderson's films is routed now in his reality.

It's of no surprise the Coppola made a film about a French aristocrat who famously said of their starving subjects, “let the eat cake”, whilst Anderson makes film with the backdrop of war but chooses to tell the story of some beautifully shot symmetrically framed iced fancies. Or that he often chooses from a small cabal of friend actors to star in his movies, who then mostly act in the same knowingly stilted fashion. There's always seemed to be a disconnect between Anderson and reality and you don’t watch his movies expecting some gritty slice of life representation of the working classes, but they definitely seem to be drifting further and further into some clique, opulent cloud of nonsense where everything is beautiful but utterly empty.

Ironically this comment is extremely ill-informed:

Picasso was a successful painter, sculptor, printmaker, and ceramicist 

Rembrandt is described as “An innovative and prolific master in three media” on his Wikipedia page- painter, printmaker, and draughtsmen 

Bob Dylan made music AND wrote poetry 

Voltaire wrote across many different genres, he was a writer, satirist, philosopher, and historian

I'm a native English speaker and I honestly had to watch Asteroid City with the subtitles on, because the dialogue is so quick and the delivery is so affected and "staccato".

That being said, it's probably my favorite Wes Anderson film among any of his recent works and I thought it had quite a bit more emotional depth than most of his films, which is something that's always prevented me from connecting with a lot of them, past an admiration for his craft and the performances of the actors.


I would definitely suggest revisiting it with subtitles and an open mind.

I'm with you in that I don't think *Asteroid City* was a complete success; it's my least favorite of his in a long time (although the other one I didn't connect with was *The Darjeeling Limited*, which you've said you love).

I think a couple of things here: both *Asteroid City* and *The French Dispatch* are actually quite experimental for him. Yes, he's maintained, perhaps doubled down on his signature aesthetic and directorial style, but that doesn't mean he's not evolving as a filmmaker. He's mainly been changing up the narrative style of his movies, rather than the visual or aesthetic ones.

The former is probably his most explicitly meta film, relying on a framing narrative that explicitly sucks out a degree of the verisimilitude of the movie. He used a similar technique in *The Grand Budapest Hotel*, but there it was unobtrusive - as soon as we're inside the storybook world, it's our "reality" as the audience member until the story ends and we get a couple of scenes returning to our reality. *Asteroid* keeps us keenly aware of the fact that it's artificial the entire time, and the emotional crux of the movie hinges on an indirect meta storytelling technique (you know the one I mean). It didn't quite work for me, but in the context of his career, I'm glad he's doing it.

You’ll never defend it from people like OP who have turned off their brains in advance and want to call it Assturd City, but it’s one of my top 3 of the year as well. Incredibly moving, makes me cry every time.

The French Dispatch on the other hand, is an anthology, and one that is very loosely tied together. I personally loved it and rank it high in his canon, but I can understand how they can come off as twee or slight because the individual segments are much less than feature length and don't necessarily share the same themes. You need to be dialled in to the segments to really feel them, and you have less time to do that; also, you're thrown into the next without being given time to process the last.

But it's definitely not emotionally hollow - the Chalamet segment was a beautiful paean to the romance of youth and revolution, even when they're doomed, and the chef segment was a fun crime story that became a powerful commentary on outsiders. It benefits from rewatches; it wasn't until my second viewing that I realized if there was one uniting thread binding the movie together, it's that it's a tribute to the kinds of publications like *The New Yorker*, and more pointedly, the editors that run them, for serving as a platform to shine a light on these small human interest stories that do have tremendous weight when you dig into them. Murray's character is the thread - he appears in all the segments (including Owen Wilson's introductory one), and in each, he shows how much support and trust he extends his writers, all because he believes in the cause. It's in line with Fiennes' character's ideology in *The Grand Budapest Hotel*.

but they seem almost like throwaway lines when they happen.  It would make sense to me if they spent any amount of time talking about who/what died and how it made them feel.  But they dont.  They just say the something has died and then move on.  

In The Darjeeling Limited, its a random ass snake that Owen Wilson finds or buys or something.  When they are all getting thrown off the train he asks, "hey what about my snake?" and the train guy, in the most flippant possible way just says, "its dead." and then closes the door on them. 

I dont even think Owen Wilson says so much as, "dang now I dont have a snake."  Everybody just shrugs it off and they move along.  Its so unusual and being that it pervades all or nearly all of his movies it makes me feel like there is something very deliberate happening there.

Yeah... we all love Picasso's sculptures so much that he never had an exhibit of his sculptures until he was 85.

I totally have a Picasso sculpture next to my Bob Dylan book of poetry right now, actually.  Legendary.

I've only kinda liked his films until Asteroid City, which i love. I always found his other films boring, but I love movies that play with structure. I like having the extra layer of trying to figure out how the nesting dolls fit together, only to realize in the end that it doesn't matter how, i just love that all the layers are there. Especially loved the balcony scene at the end and the chanting. Different strokes for different folks...

I find his last few films are less accessible for wider audiences. I feel like each film gets more complex and mature and the people who enjoyed the simpler stories in his earlier work are disappointed by that. His characters in early works were more caricature, in the newer films they are much more complex than that.
Waow.

His problem is Roman Coppola. Roman thinks that he is terribly, terribly clever and a writer who can transcend simple narrative by getting “conceptual” and outthinking it, because he’s that good.

He isn’t. And never had been.

His best movie, ”CQ,” is a style-over-substance riot of half-formed ideas: he wants to make an arty film about being personally adrift in a creative industry while your dreams are dying and your life is falling apart. But he doesn’t have skill or emotional depth to pull it off. 

The other half is a gorgeous, delightful rip-shit-riot celebration of *Barbarella* and *Diabolik*, which is clearly the movie he *wants* to make, but because he wants to be taken Seriously as an Artist, he felt he had to construct an elaborate narrative that adds almost nothing.

Sound familiar?
No but Woody Allen had a little range.

Range is great.  I do appreciate it.  I'm not trying to imply it has no value.

But I do take issue with this:

>I think the mark of a good director is when they do a good job with different genres.

And Kubrick, for what it's worth, is my very favorite director.  It's not because of his range though.  Kubrick coulda only made sci-fi films and he'd still be my favorite director...
Calling it that is acting like a 13 year-old.

>Maybe it's because I've never gotten the sense that his movies as of late are really reckoning with much of anything.

Is that always a prerequisite for a good movie, though?

There's a ton of comments here, and I haven't read them all, so I apologize if I'm repeating anything that people have said. 

In general, I agree. He's a gifted filmmaker and a pretty good writer (obviously better with partners) but the biggest issue is that he returns time and again to the overall theme of "fathers are terrible people." That worked great in some of his early stuff but it's just worn out by now, and when you combine that with weaker scripts, you start to have see the decline in his filmography. For my money, "The Grand Budapest Hotel" and his animated films are the bright spots over the last two decades.

>I think the mark of a good director is when they do a good job with different genres.  


I'd bring up Ozu as perhaps the most obvious counterexample. 

And any documentarian.
Glad someone said it. Wes has not produced a bad film maybe ever imo and his work, although becoming more auteur is still extremely high quality
What about *The Royal Tenenbaums*? To me, that movie has some real emotional moments.

>style-over-substance 

To play devil's advocate:

Isn't there an argument to be made that in cinema, which is essentially a sensory/sensual experience, style **is** substance?
Dylan very famously changed when he went electric…

Oh, sure. Bava’s Diabolik is that, but it’s *about* that. CQ takes the trappings of that idea, but sweatily tries to justify why what it’s doing isn’t silly or lame, like in the last Spider-Man movie where the make fun of Doc Ock’s real time.

If you’re gonna be about it, be about it, in other words.

The issue is Anderson’s characters are in some sort of fantasy world where every single person behaves exactly the same (I guess you could call it “repressed” but I see it as a sort of affect, a part of the visual style). There are a few stories where this works but he seems to use it in every situation and it’s just getting old. Nobody was calling for more emotion early in his career because his shtick was interesting. A lot of people, myself included, are just tired of it and want to see another side of him.
Sorry, my eyes must be getting bad. Did you say WES ANDERSON is not trying to attract attention to his style?
In this movie, yes, absolutely. You'll only understand the story when you'll realize the aesthetic is a distraction nobody needs.
The snake is revealed to be alive in the homestretch, though, depending on how you interpret that sequence.

I know that I need to get over my Wilson aversion and see it. I have stayed deliberately ignorant about it all these years because I know I’ll watch it someday and want to go in knowing nothing. I’m not going to skip a movie that has Gene Hackman and Anjelica Huston in it. I’ll try to watch it over the holidays.

>I feel like he kinda peaked with Grand Budapest hotel

I feel like that was rock bottom for him! It's just cameo after cameo with no time to dig into story, and then it just ends. Asteroid City looks promising to me (haven't seen it) with a little simplification of the cast size.
How is it not trying to draw attention to itself, yet it's a distraction? That's literally what a distraction is.

This is just wrong though. There is a surface level stylistic similarity to performances to make them all feel a part of his meticulously constructed worlds, but there is a wide range of character types on display in all of his movies.

Style is part of the substance though - style is crucial to the meaning and interpretation of his film. His characters have always lived in dollhouses. This is only more apparent in Asteroid City, where the characters are basically living inside of a play. It’s a nod to mid century American experimental theater, where form is not meant to be hid behind the suspension of disbelief, but a visible and meaningful part of the art itself.

He found his niche and stagnated within his own comfort zone. This happens fairly often with artists who maintain a reliable level of financial success without a greater need for introspection or evolution.

 I gave up with French Dispatch, or really Isle of Dogs honestly. I can give a director a pass usually but even with Hateful Eight, Licorice Pizza, Beau is Afraid, I'm really sick of going out on a limb to follow some directors random self indulgence I just can't pretend to be interested in anymore. All of the above *could* win me back but until then there's far too many superior films from older filmmakers, or foreign stuff, for me to waste time on masturbatory bullshit.

You are largely correct, FWIW the only movie that I felt explored W Anderson's limousine liberal psyche in any remotely introspective way was The Darjeeling Limited, which still has layers of ironic distance and has his usual weird dissonance, like a random Indian kids funeral being set to The Kinks or whatever. 

From what I remember that movie and Zissou (another one I think is pretty great) didn't do as well commercially or critically, and still aren't recognized among his filmography as much as they should. So maybe he had a Tarantino/Jackie Brown situation? Where Tarantino said fuck it and doubled down by making Kill Bill, when the mature, introspective stuff turned off his core audience.
"Some artifice" is a massive understatement for a movie with miniature trains and a random stop motion alien. Let alone something as cartoonish as Royal Tenenbaums..

I feel like Zissou and Darjeeling are actually the two that have the most going on below the surface oddly. Though it's been a while so I'm not sure exactly how to explain why

I think all movies are emotional, but they just show it in different days, in WA's films, the emotion is atypical, very light, quirky/individualistic, dial-downed to such an extent that it looks empty almost.. but, can there ever be art without emotion? :) I remember Rushmore and certain scenes from French Dispatch felt emotional as a viewer.. but the emotion in characters, or the quirkiness of characters is very refreshing to me.. 

What I had felt though however, overall about his films is.. WA creates a carefully crafted beautiful unreal world, a world that is unique to him, and in that world, it's like almost an intelligent artful child that is setting up a dollhouse and making the characters play... it feels like he pulls the strings of their emotions as he wishes to, and are only "presented" a certain way, but surely, there is no dearth of emotion, in my eyes atleast.
